slides.title: Read the Update
slides.caption: X_{k+1}=1.5X_k-0.5X_kX_k^TX_k
slides.narration: First form the Gram matrix X_k transpose X_k, then multiply it on the left by X_k. That makes the cubic term X_k X_k transpose X_k.

slides.title: Choose X_0
slides.caption: X_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.2&0\\0&0.8\end{bmatrix}
slides.narration: We choose a diagonal starting matrix. Its diagonal entries, and therefore its singular values, are 1.2 and 0.8.

slides.title: Form the Gram Matrix
slides.caption: X_0^TX_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.44&0\\0&0.64\end{bmatrix}
slides.narration: The matrix is diagonal and symmetric, so its transpose is itself. Squaring the diagonal entries gives 1.44 and 0.64.

slides.title: Build the Cubic Term
slides.caption: X_0X_0^TX_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.728&0\\0&0.512\end{bmatrix}
slides.narration: Multiplying X_0 by the Gram matrix once more produces the cubic diagonal values 1.728 and 0.512.

slides.title: Make the First Update
slides.caption: X_1=\begin{bmatrix}0.936&0\\0&0.944\end{bmatrix}
slides.narration: Scale X_0 by 1.5, subtract half of the cubic term, and obtain X_1. Both diagonal values move closer to 1.

slides.title: What the SVD Reveals
slides.caption: X_k=U\Sigma_kV^T\Longrightarrow X_kX_k^TX_k=U\Sigma_k^3V^T
slides.narration: The SVD shows that the singular vectors U and V stay fixed. Each singular value is transformed independently by the same cubic scalar rule.

slides.title: Track Two Singular Values
slides.caption: \sigma_{k+1}=1.5\sigma_k-0.5\sigma_k^3
slides.narration: The value starting above 1 decreases, while the value starting below 1 increases. After two updates they are both already near 1.

slides.title: Convergence to One
slides.caption: \sigma_{1,k},\sigma_{2,k}\to1
slides.narration: Continuing the iteration, both singular values rapidly approach 1. By iteration 4 the remaining error is tiny, and the displayed values round to 1 by iteration 5.

slides.title: Why One Is Special
slides.caption: f(\sigma)=1.5\sigma-0.5\sigma^3,\quad f(1)=1,\quad f'(1)=0
slides.narration: One is a fixed point because f of 1 equals 1. Also, the derivative at 1 is zero, so the linear error term disappears and convergence accelerates.

slides.title: The Orthogonal Limit
slides.caption: X_k\to I_2,\qquad I_2^TI_2=I_2
slides.narration: For this diagonal example, the singular vectors remain unchanged, so the matrix approaches the identity. The identity is orthogonal because its transpose times itself is the identity.

slides.title: Final Answer
slides.caption: \boxed{\sigma_{k+1}=1.5\sigma_k-0.5\sigma_k^3,\qquad X_{k+1}=1.5X_k-0.5X_kX_k^TX_k,\qquad X_k\to UV^T}
slides.narration: In general, every singular value follows the cubic scalar map. When they all converge to 1, the matrix converges to U V transpose, an orthogonal matrix; here that limit is the identity.
